title: Longest Reading Streak
story: A reading app numbers days from its launch: day 0 is launch day, day 1 the day after, and people who tested it early have negative days. Every time you read, the app logs the day number. The log syncs from your phone and your tablet, so it arrives jumbled, and a day you read twice appears twice.
The app wants to show your best ever streak: the longest run of back-to-back days on which you read at least once.
task: Write longestStreak(days). Return the length of the longest run of consecutive whole numbers d, d + 1, ..., d + L - 1 that all appear in days. Repeated day numbers count once.
An empty log returns 0. Aim for O(n) time: sorting works but costs O(n log n).

examples.explanation: Days 10, 11, 12, 13 make a streak of 4. Days 3, 4, 5 make a streak of 3. Day 11 appears twice, but it is still one day, so the answer is 4, not 5.
Days -2, -1, 0, 1 are back to back, a streak of 4 that runs across launch day. Day 7 stands alone.
No reading at all, so the best streak is 0.

hints: In the first example, which day numbers could be the first day of a streak? What is true about the day before each of them?
A day d starts a streak exactly when d - 1 is not in the log. Days 3 and 10 start streaks; days 4, 5, 11, 12 and 13 do not.

If you could ask "is this day in the log?" in one step, then from each starting day you could count upward until the streak breaks. Which structure answers that question in one step, and also removes the duplicates?

Put every day into a hash set. For each day d in the set, skip it if d - 1 is also in the set. Otherwise count d, d + 1, d + 2, ... while they are in the set, and keep the longest count. Because counting only starts at streak beginnings, every day is counted once.
bruteForce: For each day, count upward from it, checking whether d + 1, d + 2 and so on appear by scanning the log each time.

Each check is a scan of n entries, and a single long streak gets recounted from every one of its days. That is O(n³) in the worst case, hopeless for 100,000 entries. Even with a set to make each check O(1), starting from every day still recounts a streak of length L about L²/2 times: one streak of 100,000 days costs 5 billion steps.

js: * @param {number[]} days  day numbers, in any order, repeats allowed
* @return {number} length of the longest run of consecutive days

tests.note: repeat inside a streak must not break it: defeats a sort-and-scan that resets on equal neighbours
repeats must not lengthen a streak: defeats a sort-and-scan that counts equal neighbours
extreme values: no array indexed by day
one streak of 10 with repeats, unsorted

js: const logged = new Set(days); // also drops repeated days
if (logged.has(d - 1)) continue; // not the first day of a streak
py: logged = set(days)  # also drops repeated days
if d - 1 in logged:  # not the first day of a streak
walkthrough: Two ideas fit together here. First, a hash set lets you ask "did I read on day x?" in one step, and it removes repeats for free. Second, only count a streak from its first day, the one whose previous day is missing. Then each streak is walked exactly once.
• 12: 11 is in the set, so 12 is mid-streak. Skip.
• 10: 9 is missing, so 10 starts a streak. Count 11, 12, 13 (all present), then 14 is missing. Length 4. best = 4.
• 5 and 11 and 13: each has its previous day in the set. Skip.
• 3: 2 is missing, so count up: 4, 5, then 6 is missing. Length 3. best stays 4.

Why is this O(n) when there is a loop inside a loop? The inner while only runs from streak starts, and each day belongs to exactly one streak. So across the whole run, the inner loop steps over each day once. Loop over the set, not the original list, or a repeated starting day would recount its whole streak.
solution.timeWhy: Building the set is O(n), and each day is visited once by the outer loop and at most once by an inner count.
solution.spaceWhy: The set holds every distinct day.
solution.takeaway: Turning a list into a hash set gives you O(1) membership tests. Combine that with "only start from the beginning of a run" (check that the previous element is missing) and nested-looking loops become linear.
